newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Weary Romanians set to give mixed election verdict.
newsitem.headline: Weary Romanians set to give mixed election verdict.

text.p: Romanians, wearied by seven years of economic malaise, appear set to give President Ion Iliescu lukewarm backing in Sunday's elections but reject his leftist party and return a parliament demanding faster reforms.
With a campaigning ban in force shoppers on Friday replaced campaign activists who had thronged Bucharest's tree-lined boulevards in two days of competing rallies.
The government, keen to reassure voters that all will be well in the winter, announced there were sufficient energy reserves to prevent a repeat of last year's power shortages.

Iliescu, in power since the fall of communism in 1989, heads most opinion polls with just over 30 percent, about four ahead of his nearest rival, academic Emil Constantinescu. A run-off round later this month is virtually certain.
But voters were turning away from his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), made up of former communists, which lies second in polls for parliamentary elections also due on Sunday.

Tough coalition talks will follow Sunday's vote. Analysts speculate Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) and ex-premier Petre Roman's Social Democratic Union (USD) could join to push the PDSR into their first spell in opposition.
In a television debate on Thursday Iliescu urged voters to stick with his moderate approach and ignore rivals who denounce him as a vestige of the Communist era.
"Those who say nothing has changed ought to look around," he said. "We cannot start from scratch every day. We cannot allow what our government has built to be destroyed."
Romania, impoverished under communism, has seen no significant economic recovery since the 1989 execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Outmoded industry remains subsidised, inflation is over target, currency markets are subject to controls and credits have been suspended by the International Monetary Fund.

Dutch finance minister Gerrit Zalm, which represents Romanian interests on the IMF's executive board, said this week any new government would have to cut spending and let the local currency float freely to secure resumed support.
Opposition parties have seized on plunging living standards and say Romania has lagged behind Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic because of Iliescu's half-hearted embrace of reforms.
Iliescu says his programme of gradual change has protected workers from unemployment and prevented social chaos.

The PDSR government made further efforts on Friday to dispell its reputation for corruption and mismanagement with the Industry Ministry assuring the press steps have been taken to ensure light and heat for all this winter.

But voters, particularly in urban areas, appear to distrust the PDSR. Its hold is strongest in the countryside and its best chance of retaining power rests with persuading its current opponents to join it in a coalition.
The CDR and USD both deny they will work with the PDSR but neither has yet announced a post-election strategy.
Iliescu won two previous elections handily in 1990 and 1992 and says he is happy to work within a French-style "cohabitation" arrangement with opposition parties.
"It will not be easy to form a coalition as the election is sure to be close," said political analyst Alina Mungiu.
"A coalition between the ruling party and the CDR is still most likely. Iliescu has the means to do this and not everyone in the CDR is quite as firm in refusing a coalition."
The opposition has combined so far only to guard against what it says are PDSR attempts to rig the outcome of the vote.

Problems have already been reported in the country's complex electoral system. Two members of the central election authority said that up to six million ballots would have to be reprinted at the weekend to correct errors.
